body:
## Features

- **Scheduled publishing**: the post-save dialog gains an [s] choice that asks for a date and time directly; `./blog.sh schedule <slug>` covers already future-dated drafts, and the new `publish-scheduled.sh` cron publishes due drafts with their scheduled date kept, announcement included. `lib/publishing.rb` extracts the publish/announce mechanics so the CLI (all prompts) and the cron (none) can't drift apart.
- **Bluesky as a comments network**: a site now configures exactly one of `mastodon:` / `bluesky:` -- announce (300-grapheme composition, link+hashtag facets with byte offsets), client-side comments from the public AppView, stats, unpublish-delete and a `bluesky` resend command, all mirroring the Mastodon flows. Posts store `bluesky_url` + `bluesky_uri`.
- **Two new sidebar widgets**: recent Bluesky posts (public AppView, handle falls back to `bluesky.handle`) and a generic RSS/Atom feed widget (both dialects autodetected).
- **Six more built-in social icons** (bluesky, instagram, threads, youtube, rss, email) and a richer social example config.
- **Config consolidation**: `widgets.toots.instance` falls back to `mastodon.instance`; optional `mastodon.toot_length` and `site.page_size` knobs with unchanged defaults.

## Investigations recorded in the roadmap

X rejected for both comments and widgets (pay-per-use API since February 2026; the RSS widget covers X via a self-hosted Nitter). Threads feasible for both via its free API but deferred (Meta app + OAuth + 60-day token refresh friction). Instagram has no usable read API.

## Docs

Install/operations/architecture/decisions updated throughout; the README names both comment networks and carries a Bluesky badge.

author: dknauss
body:
## Summary

- keep classic admin expiry reloads while preserving unsaved block-editor work
- withdraw the stale editor timer without hiding its live expiry announcement
- restore and restart the persistent timer when the editor grants a new session
- prove the classic/editor split and expiry-to-regrant lifecycle in a real browser

## Root cause and impact

`wp-sudo-admin-bar.js` reloaded every admin page when its local countdown reached zero. The script is also enqueued in the block editor, so an unrelated Sudo expiry could navigate away from long-lived editor work. Simply suppressing the reload left the admin bar stuck at `0:00` after a later in-editor grant.

`Admin_Bar::enqueue_assets()` now derives an explicit `reload_on_expiry` flag from `WP_Screen::is_block_editor()`. Classic screens retain the existing reload. On block-editor screens, expiry hides only the stale interactive timer, preserves the `role=status` live region long enough to announce expiry, and listens to the established `wp-sudo-session-granted` event to restore/restart the timer with the server-reported duration.

## Stack order

This PR is intentionally based on #502 (`ci/482-javascript-lint`) because that PR reformats and owns the same JavaScript file. Merge #502 first, then retarget this PR to `main`; do not hand-resolve the formatter overlap.

## Validation after restack

- TDD: TIMR-05 failed before the expiry/regrant implementation.
- `composer test` — 1,309 tests, 3,911 assertions.
- `composer lint`.
- `composer analyse` — PHPStan level 6 and Psalm clean.
- `npm run lint:js`.
- `composer verify:i18n`.
- `composer verify:metrics` with untracked `node_modules` isolated; verifier gap is fixed separately by #544.
- Isolated WordPress 7.0 wp-env on unused ports: all five `admin-bar-timer.spec.ts` cases pass.
  - TIMR-04 proves classic-screen expiry still reloads.
  - TIMR-05 proves editor expiry does not navigate, the stale control is withdrawn while its live-region announcement remains, and a later grant restores the countdown.
- Current staged metrics tree approved before commit; branch is clean.

WordPress API verification: WordPress 6.4 `WP_Screen::is_block_editor()` in `wp-admin/includes/class-wp-screen.php`.

Closes #300.

author: haomingkoo
body:
The per-company cap treated a symptom, and the commit that added it said so: a decisive fix needs a spam signal, because many separate MLM outfits each post a few listings rather than one company posting many. The existing `jd_analyzer` quality score does not separate them on its own — spam mean 70.5 against 79.1 for normal, heavily overlapping.

## The signal

Emoji and hashtags **in a title** carry it. A real employer writing "Senior Platform Engineer" does not reach for 🎯. Phrase tells (`no experience needed`, `weekly pay`, `urgent`, `fast promotion`) are weighted lower, since each appears innocently and one alone must not condemn a job.

**654 of 16,390 flagged (4.0%).** Top companies: SIMPLE RECRUIT, ROYAL ORG, EMINENCE ORGANIZATION, GROWTH SYNDICATE, BRANDOVA, THRIVE ORGANIZATION. Four of those were named independently in the original production audit of page 1, so the signal rediscovers the companies that caused the complaint rather than being fitted to them.

## Company rollup, keyed on ratio not count

A single emoji title is weak evidence; a company where most postings carry the tells is an outfit, and its plain-titled listings are the same operation in a quieter title.

This must be a **ratio**. Measured: a count rule taints RECRUIT EXPRESS — 608 postings, 12 flagged, **2%** — a real agency that would have had 596 genuine jobs buried. At 50% the caught set is 11 companies, every one an MLM-style outfit, picking up **89 quiet postings**. Thresholds measured across 30/40/50/60% and exposed as config.

## Ranking

Demoted, not dropped, for the same reason as the company cap: a promotional posting is still a real job someone may want. `exclude_promotional=true` is offered separately for candidates who want them gone.

This is a **different axis** from `direct_employers_only` and does not replace it — the heaviest promotional posters are legitimately direct employers, which is why the original test found `direct_employers_only=true` still left 18 of 20 page-one listings flagged. On the corpus the two filters cut 16,390 to 9,327 and 15,736 respectively, and to 8,954 together.

**Measured:** the first promotional posting sits at **rank 23** under `sort=newest` and **beyond rank 600** under balanced.

## Bugs found while verifying, all silent

- `_precompute_batch` copies `apply_job_precomputes`' output back field by field and never assigned `promotional_score`. The backfill ran, logged "Precomputed 15000 jobs", and wrote zeros.
- The precompute marker gates a one-time full pass, so an existing deployment would never backfill a new column. Bumped to v2; a default of `0` is indistinguishable from "not yet computed", so there is no missing-value condition to detect instead.
- `func.max(a, b)` is a scalar in SQLite but an **aggregate** in Postgres. It would have passed every local test and failed in production. Now a portable `case()`.

## roborev findings, addressed

An independent review of this branch found three more:

- The rollup only ran from its admin endpoint, so it went stale after every crawl. Now runs after the precompute backfill.
- A qualifying company stored its raw percentage, and that value doubles as the demotion signal, so a ratio tuned below the threshold meant a company could qualify and still demote nothing. Qualifying companies are floored at the threshold.
- The two config constants were declared twice. Deduplicated.

## Verification

823 backend tests, ruff, compileall. Verified on a pristine 220MB DB: both migrations apply, 654 scored, 11 companies tainted, 89 quiet postings caught. An earlier version of the detector matched non-ASCII and wrongly flagged 1,231 ordinary titles like "Project Manager (Electrical – Data Centre)" — those are en-dashes, not emoji, and a test now pins that such a title scores zero.

**Post-deploy:** `POST /api/admin/rollup-company-promotional` (also runs automatically after the startup backfill).

author: mgilbir
body:
PR 5 of a stacked series. Base is `audit/04-validator-harness`.

Addresses audit finding **C4** (High), design tension **D4**, and the `Validate`
half of **C7**.

## The problem

`Profile` was documented as six values "in increasing data richness", the last
being `ProfileXRechnung`. The argument selected almost nothing:
`validateEN16931` consults it in exactly three predicates (`== ProfileMinimum`,
`== ProfileBasicWL`, `== ProfileExtended`) and never validated it.

| `profile` | rules on the same document |
|---|---|
| `ProfileEN16931` | 16 |
| `ProfileXRechnung` | 16 — identical set |
| `ProfileBasic` / `ProfileExtended` | 16 — identical set |
| `ProfileMinimum` | 11 |
| `Profile("GARBAGE")` | 16 — identical set |

So `Validate(ctx, xml, ProfileXRechnung)` applied zero `BR-DE-*` rules — the
call that looked most like "validate this as XRechnung" validated it least — and
`Profile("EN16931")`, one space from the constant and the exact spelling
`ProfileFor` takes as *input*, was silently read as EN 16931.

## What changed

**`ProfileXRechnung` is removed.** XRechnung is a national CIUS, not a
data-richness tier, and it was already reachable correctly two other ways
(`ValidateXRechnung`; `ValidateCIUS` routing on BT-24 to `CIUSXRechnung`).
Representing it a third time inside the richness enum is what created the trap.

The claim that it was behaviourally identical to `ProfileEN16931` was verified,
not assumed: across the 900 EN 16931-parseable documents in `testdata`,
`validateEN16931` at each of the two profiles produced identical finding sets,
document for document. (Two documents appeared to differ on a first pass; that
was map-iteration ordering, and the same ordering varies between two runs at a
single profile.) `validateXRechnung` now passes `ProfileEN16931`, and the
XRechnung FP=0 oracle is unchanged at 86/86.

**`ProfileFor("XRECHNUNG")` now reports false, and `CIUSFor` is added.**
`ProfileFor` maps XMP `ConformanceLevel` strings for a PDF caller, and
`XRECHNUNG` is a level ZUGFeRD 2.x producers really do write, so dropping it
outright would lose information. `CIUSFor` is its companion over the same input,
matched the same way: `ProfileFor` answers how rich the data claims to be,
`CIUSFor` which national rule set it claims to follow, and exactly one of the two
reports true for any level either recognises. It returns the `CIUS` that
`ValidateCIUS` routes on, so the caller lands on a validator that applies the
`BR-DE-*` rules.

**An unrecognised `Profile` is refused, under a new reserved rule identifier
`RuleProfile` (`"profile"`), with `SourceChecker`.** The run validates nothing
and returns exactly that one finding. Each alternative was worse: `RuleSyntax`
would accuse a document that was never examined; `RuleLimit` is documented as a
resource-budget or cancellation event and its identifier is shared verbatim with
the `pdf0` sibling module, so a caller routing "retry it smaller" would retry
forever; an empty slice would let `len(v) == 0` read as "valid", the one outcome
this package refuses everywhere else.

`IsCheckerViolation` recognises it. Widening is safe in the direction the doc
comment cares about — `pdf0` never emits `RuleProfile`, so nothing that exists
today changes classification — and *not* widening would leave a caller filtering
with the predicate counting its own bad argument as a document defect.
`RuleSyntax` stays deliberately outside: "this file is not well-formed" is a
finding about the document, and a definite one.

`Validate` is the only exported entry point taking a `Profile`; the CIUS and
national validators select their rule set from the document.

**C7, in passing:** `Validate` carried two stacked doc comments, both printed by
`go doc`, the first naming `ValidateFacturX` (not in this module) and hedging
that the profile lets rules "be applied as the rule set grows". The orphan is
deleted; the survivor states what `profile` does and does not do. The
package-clause and README defects in C7 are left for PR 9.

## API breakage

- `ProfileXRechnung` removed; `Profile` now has five values
- `ProfileFor("XRECHNUNG")` reports `("", false)`
- `CIUSFor(level string) (CIUS, bool)` added
- `RuleProfile` added; `IsCheckerViolation` returns true for it
- `Validate` no longer treats an unrecognised `Profile` as EN 16931

## Tests

New assertions, each **verified to fail when run against the parent commit's
API** (rewritten there so they could actually execute rather than merely fail to
compile):

- an unknown, empty, mistyped or `"XRECHNUNG"` profile yields exactly one
  `SourceChecker`/`RuleProfile` finding — never zero, never `RuleSyntax`, and
  `IsCheckerViolation` true
- the refusal precedes reading the document: malformed XML under an unknown
  profile reports the profile, not the syntax
- `ProfileFor` and `CIUSFor` partition the `ConformanceLevel` space

Plus pins for the differences that are *real*, so a future change cannot flatten
one the way `ProfileXRechnung` was flat. Each was confirmed to fail when its gate
in `validateEN16931` is removed: MINIMUM's reduced set (BR-10, BR-11, BR-CO-16,
BR-CO-18), MINIMUM/BASIC WL head-only gating (BR-12, BR-16), EXTENDED's
BR-CO-11/12 exemption, and that BASIC / EN 16931 / EXTENDED differ in nothing
else.

## Oracles

```
checked 1613 documents against the tree reference
EN 16931 conformance: 0 false positives, 198/198 rules caught (baseline 198)
NLCIUS conformance: 27 error instances caught, 0 false positives
Peppol corpus: 9/9 examples clean (FP=0)
XRechnung corpus: 86/86 instances clean (FP=0)
```

`gofmt -l .` silent, `go vet ./...` clean, `go test ./... -count=1` green:
100 top-level tests, 0 skips, 0 failures.

author: toinevl
body:
Completes wishlist #32. `alicante` now runs on **F1 Free** — verified `/login` 200 on first request, `/api/teams` and `/` still 307 to `/login`, so auth survived the migration.

## Two corrections to the plan I gave

1. **`az webapp update --plan` does not exist** on CLI 2.88.0. The move is `--set serverFarmId=<plan resource id>`.

2. With that fixed it still failed — `Conflict 59602, "due to hosting constraints"`. A site can only move between plans in the same **webspace**, and a webspace is bound to the resource group that owns the plan. `alicante`'s webspace is `rgWebsite-PolandCentralwebspace-Linux` because its plan has always lived in `rgWebsite`; the F1 plan I created in `rgWorkforcePlan` landed in a different webspace and could never host it. Resolved by creating `wfp-plan-free` in **rgWebsite**, and deleting the `rgWorkforcePlan` copy rather than leaving another empty plan behind.

## Consequence for the IaC

`main.bicep` creates its plan in `rgWorkforcePlan`, so deploying it produces a plan that **cannot host this site** — an empty plan, which is exactly the waste #31 just removed. Added a warning comment at the module and opened **#35** for the real fix: recreating the site in this resource group's webspace, which costs a new default hostname, Entra redirect URI updates, and a fresh package URL.

author: sduranc
body:
## Problem

v1.7.0 mirrors workloads (Deployment/StatefulSet/DaemonSet) with `images` projected, but their `revision` is empty — the console cannot build release history for workload apps (e.g. dis-console itself on the admin clusters: bare Deployments applied by the root Kustomization). The UI already treats the primary image tag as a workload's release identity, but derives it client-side, so the status-event history never records image bumps.

## Fix (agent-side only, no schema bump)

- `applyWorkloadStatus` sets `revision` to the primary container's image tag for all three kinds — the container named like the workload, else the first — parsed with `github.com/distribution/reference` (the grammar kubelet admits refs with): tag when present, 12-char short digest for digest-only refs, `latest` for bare refs, empty for refs kubelet would reject as `InvalidImageName`.
- The upsert's `updated_at` CASE gains `revision`: on rollout, existing workload rows receive the tag under an unchanged content hash (the pod template was already hashed), and without the comparison the central pull (`updated_at > cursor`) would never mirror the backfill — same class as the appliedBy backfill (#3812). Steady-state is quiet since revision is deterministic from hashed content for every kind.
- Status events already snapshot revision transitions, so image bumps land in history as releases from rollout onward.

Dependency delta: `distribution/reference v0.6.0` + `opencontainers/go-digest v1.0.0` (indirect); both effectively frozen upstream, Renovate will track them.

Also bumps indirect `golang.org/x/text` v0.38.0 → v0.39.0: Trivy flags CVE-2026-56852 (HIGH) there since the CVE entered the DB after the v1.7.1 release build — pre-existing on main, but a red scan would block release-main from publishing the patch release this change rides.

## Verification

- `make run-checks-ci-cache` — green (tag-parsing table + per-kind revision assertions)
- `make test-e2e-kind-ci` — green; new store tests assert the backfill advances `updated_at` exactly once and an image bump writes the history event through the server copy path (`EventsSince`)

## Rollout

Patch release. After release-please cuts it, bump the agents like #3843; the server needs nothing (central `Apply` copies revision unconditionally) but gets bumped for tidiness.

author: luishreyes
body:
Primer taller del semestre, el del jueves de la semana 2. El enunciado estaba bien planteado; la solución tenía errores técnicos que habrían llevado a calificar mal.

## Por qué el visor

El PFD es un mapa de bits de 2843 px incrustado en un PDF. A tamaño de página varias etiquetas no se distinguen, y de ahí salieron casi todos los errores de la solución anterior: se reportaba que el mezclador no estaba rotulado (es M-101) y que el diagrama no tenía bombas (tiene tres, P-101, P-201 y P-301). El enunciado ahora abre el diagrama a pantalla completa con zoom de rueda, arrastre, doble clic, botones y cierre con Esc, todo incrustado en el mismo HTML.

## Correcciones de fondo

| Antes | Ahora |
|---|---|
| «En la corriente 9 no debería salir etanol» | El etanol sí se arrastra con el CO2, del orden del 1,4 % de la producción. No es error |
| «T-201 es innecesario» | Es la práctica estándar en destilerías. No es error |
| «Falta un equipo entre 17 y 18» | Es un tee. Lo que falta es la bomba del acumulador |
| «El mezclador no está rotulado» | Es M-101, visible con zoom |
| El reflujo lo hace posible «una válvula» | La carga hidrostática, que en este dibujo no existe: falta la bomba de reflujo |
| Bomba axial para alimentar la columna | Centrífuga. La axial es de caudal alto y cabeza muy baja |
| No se daba el valor del azeótropo | 95,6 % p/p, 89,5 % molar, 97,2 % v/v, a 78,2 °C |

## Formulación

Los puntos sumaban 90 y ahora suman 100, con una parte de formato que recoge las exigencias que ya estaban en los entregables. El bono pasa a un criterio verificable: 13 de 15 errores de una lista cerrada, con descuento por señalar como error algo que está bien dibujado. Y se dice explícitamente que el trabajo continúa en casa, que es como funcionan las sesiones de jueves.

## Qué entra aquí y qué no

Entra el enunciado en HTML con su PDF y el diagrama suelto. **La solución no**: es confidencial y vive solo en la carpeta del curso, junto con los tres archivos originales, que quedan archivados en `_original/`.

El rótulo del PFD traía nombre y código de un estudiante de un semestre anterior. Quedó anonimizado antes de publicar.

## Cambios de código

`category` admite ahora `'taller'`, y la hoja de la semana rotula el ítem como Taller en vez de Guía.

## Verificación

- El visor se ejercitó con Playwright: abre, hace zoom de 100 % a 332 %, cierra con Esc y restituye el desplazamiento de la página. Sin errores de consola.
- Los dos PDF se regeneraron; en papel el pie del diagrama cambia y remite a la versión en línea.
- `npm run build` pasa.

author: aderonkeafolabi
body:
Closes #749

`apps/api/package.json`'s `test:integration` script named exact test
filenames instead of a glob pattern. By the time of implementation it had
already grown to two hardcoded names
(`src/__tests__/integration/bonds.test.ts` and
`src/__tests__/integration/importer-documents-view.test.ts`) — but two
*more* test files already existed on disk
(`src/__tests__/integration/ein-hash.test.ts` and
`src/__tests__/integration/health-db.test.ts`) that were silently never
executed in CI, because nobody had gone back to add their names to the
script. This is exactly the failure mode the issue describes: any future
contributor who adds a new test file under `src/__tests__/` gets a false
sense that it's running in CI, when it silently isn't.

This PR (#749) replaces the hardcoded file list with a quoted glob pattern:
```
"src/__tests__/**/*.test.ts"
```
so every current and future `*.test.ts` file under `apps/api/src/__tests__/`
is picked up automatically. The pattern is quoted to avoid shell/npm
expansion inconsistencies — an unquoted glob in an npm script is a known
footgun that fails to resolve to any files on some platforms/shells (Node's
own test-runner docs recommend quoting for this reason).

I verified locally that the glob mechanism works exactly as intended: I
added a temporary smoke-test file
(`src/__tests__/integration/zzz-glob-smoke.test.ts`), ran the updated
command, and confirmed all 5 files (the 4 real ones plus the smoke file)
were discovered and executed, producing a JUnit report at the same
`test-results.xml` path/format the CI workflow already uploads as an
artifact. I then deleted the smoke file — it is not part of this PR's diff.

**Convention for new integration tests:** any new API integration test
should be added under `apps/api/src/__tests__/` (any subdirectory) and
follow the existing `*.test.ts` naming convention. No script edit is
required going forward — the glob picks it up automatically.

**Flagging a pre-existing, out-of-scope compatibility note for reviewers:**
Node's `--test` CLI flag only supports glob patterns from **Node.js v21**
onward (confirmed against Node's test-runner documentation). This repo's
root `package.json` sets `"engines": { "node": ">=20" }`, and every GitHub
Actions workflow under `.github/workflows/` (15 files, including
`api-integration.yml`) pins `actions/setup-node` to `node-version: 20`. That
version pin is a repo-wide convention that predates and is unrelated to this
issue, so I deliberately did **not** change it here — changing CI Node
versions across 15 workflow files is out of scope for a `package.json`
script fix. Flagging it so a maintainer can decide whether to bump
`api-integration.yml` (or all workflows) to Node ≥21 in a follow-up PR, since
without that bump the new glob pattern may not resolve correctly on Node 20
in CI even though it resolves correctly locally on newer Node versions.

# Changed
- `apps/api/package.json`: `test:integration` script changed from two
  hardcoded filenames to the quoted glob `"src/__tests__/**/*.test.ts"`
  (issue #749)

# Testing
```bash
# From apps/api/, with a temporary smoke test file added to prove new files
# are picked up automatically:
node --import tsx/esm --test --test-reporter=junit \
  --test-reporter-destination=/tmp/test-results.xml \
  "src/__tests__/**/*.test.ts"

grep -o 'name="[^"]*test.ts"' /tmp/test-results.xml   # lists all discovered files
grep -c "<testsuite " /tmp/test-results.xml           # => 4 (after removing the smoke file)

# Smoke file removed afterward, not committed:
rm apps/api/src/__tests__/integration/zzz-glob-smoke.test.ts
```

# Scope Notes
- Only `apps/api/package.json` was changed — no test files, CI workflow
  files, or `engines` field were modified.
- The Node ≥21 CLI-glob-support vs. CI's Node 20 pin is called out above as a
  known caveat but intentionally left unfixed here, since it spans 15
  workflow files unrelated to this issue's stated scope
  (`apps/api/package.json`).
- The temporary smoke-test file used for local verification was deleted and
  is not part of the diff.

# Push Command
```bash
git push -u origin fix/749-test-integration-glob
```

author: floresaxel
body:
`.env.example` has required `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` to be URL-safe ever since the prod
compose file landed, because `docker-compose.prod.yml` interpolates it **raw** into
`postgresql://user:PASSWORD@postgres:5432/db` — a `/` (which base64 output produces
routinely) ends the URI's authority component and the whole thing stops parsing.
That requirement was a comment and nothing more.

Unguarded, the first symptom is postgres.js throwing `Invalid URL` from inside the
connection path: **api and powersync crash-loop on a fresh deploy with nothing
pointing at the password.** Not hypothetical — this machine's own `.env` held a
base64 value containing `+` and `/`, and both `new URL()` and postgres.js threw on
the URI built from it exactly as compose builds it.

## The change

`resolveDatabaseUrl()` now parses before returning and throws a FATAL that names
`POSTGRES_PASSWORD` as the suspect, with the `openssl rand -hex 32` remedy.

- **The check is the driver's own** — postgres.js also parses with WHATWG `URL` — so
  it cannot reject a URL that postgres.js would have accepted.
- **The message deliberately omits the URL**, which embeds the credential. A test
  pins that it never leaks.
- **The fallback branch is guarded too**, so a malformed `PRISMS_POSTGRES_PORT`
  fails the same clear way rather than reaching the driver.
- `powersync` is a third-party service with no equivalent guard and would still
  crash-loop, so the URL-safe rule stands. `.env.example` now says both things.

## Gate

Verified against the live compose stack after merging current `main` (which brought
in PR #12's security remediation):

| Suite | Result |
|---|---|
| `@prisms/db` | **60/60** (integration suites actually run, not skipped) |
| `apps/server` | **211/211** across 23 files vs live Postgres |
| `turbo lint typecheck test` | **21/21** |

author: arsalandotme
body:
## Summary

Quoted history in Word-generated Outlook desktop replies was not collapsed properly: only a deeply nested provider marker (e.g. `messageReplySection`) moved behind the disclosure, while the Outlook `From:/Sent:/To:/Subject:` header block, external-email banner, the full quoted previous message body, and the quoted signature stayed visible. This adds the missing marker to both collapse paths so the entire quoted chain collapses from the Outlook header downward.

## Changes

- HTML path (`HtmlMessage.tsx`): detect the Word/Outlook reply header — a `border-top` divider div whose text starts with `From:` and carries `Sent/To/Cc/Subject:` labels — lift layout-only wrapper divs, and collapse the header plus all following siblings. The earliest recognized marker in document order wins, so a `gmail_quote` wrapping such a header still collapses as one region.
- Plain-text path (`quotedHistory.ts`): split at a `From:` line when a contiguous `Sent/To/Cc/Subject:` label follows within the header block (Outlook desktop uses no `>` prefixes).
- New checked-in fixture `outlook-word-reply-section.html`: a redacted real Word/Outlook reply (based on the email that exposed the bug) preserving provider-specific nesting, attributes, and whitespace, including an embedded `messageBodySection`/`messageSignatureSection`/`messageReplySection` chain and a nested `-----Original Message-----` block.
- Adversarial coverage: header with no quoted content after it stays visible; decorative border-top dividers without mail labels are untouched; stacked Word headers collapse into a single disclosure; prose `From:` lines without adjacent labels and labels separated by blank lines do not split; expand-collapse-expand round trip through the rendered shadow DOM.

## Testing

- New regression tests fail on the previous implementation (visible region still contained `From:`/`External email`/`wrote:`; zero disclosures in the stacked-header case; no plain-text split), proving sensitivity to the defect.
- Full suite: 191/191 tests across 23 files; `tsc --noEmit` clean.
- Verified end-to-end against the real failing email body from the local store: exactly one disclosure, new reply and sender signature visible, everything from the `From:` header down collapsed.

author: frezechi9999
body:
## Summary

Closes #101

Hardens optional webhook notifications to the TrustBridge dashboard (or any external endpoint) with HMAC-SHA256 signatures, configurable timeouts, and full failure isolation so comment posting always succeeds even when the webhook fails.

---

## Changes

### New: `src/webhook.ts`
Core webhook module providing:
- `computeWebhookSignature(body, secret)` — HMAC-SHA256, returns `sha256=<hex-digest>` (same format as GitHub webhooks)
- `buildWebhookPayload(result, address, repo, issueNumber)` — constructs the signed payload; Stellar address is redacted to first-4/last-4 before leaving the process
- `deliverWebhook(payload, config, fetchFn)` — POST with `AbortController` timeout; **never throws**, returns a `WebhookDeliveryResult` with `sent`, `statusCode`, and optional `error`
- `sendWebhookNotification(...)` — high-level entry point called from `src/index.ts`; logs outcome with `core.info` / `core.warning` and isolates all errors

### Updated: `action.yml`
Three new **optional** inputs (all off by default):

| Input | Default | Description |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| `webhook_url` | ``` (empty) | HTTPS endpoint to POST signed payloads to |
| `webhook_secret` | ``` (empty) | Shared HMAC-SHA256 signing secret — never logged or embedded in comments |
| `webhook_timeout_ms` | `5000` | Per-request timeout in ms; on timeout a warning is logged and the run continues |

### Updated: `src/index.ts`
- Imports `sendWebhookNotification` from `./webhook`
- Reads `webhook_url`, `webhook_secret`, `webhook_timeout_ms` inputs
- Calls `sendWebhookNotification` after validation + comment posting; errors are isolated with `try/catch` and never block the run
- Fixes pre-existing `try {} else {}` syntax error on the comment-posting block

### New: `__tests__/webhook.test.ts`
30 tests covering:
- `computeWebhookSignature`: determinism, secret sensitivity, known HMAC-SHA256 value
- `buildWebhookPayload`: address redaction, schema version, checks array mapping, ISO-8601 timestamp
- `deliverWebhook`: success path, signature header present/absent, network error isolation, AbortError/timeout isolation, correct URL + Content-Type, signature matches body
- `sendWebhookNotification`: no-op when URL empty, never throws on failure

---

## Security design

| Threat | Defence |
|--------|---------|
| Unsigned webhooks spoofable | HMAC-SHA256 via `X-TrustBridge-Signature: sha256=<hex>` |
| Secret leakage in logs | `webhook_secret` never appears in any log line or comment |
| Slow receiver stalling the action | `AbortController` timeout (default 5 s) |
| Hard webhook failure blocking contributor comment | All errors caught and surfaced as `core.warning`; comment path continues unconditionally |
| Feature always-on | Disabled by default (`webhook_url` empty); zero overhead when not configured |

---

## Payload schema

```json
{
  "schema_version": "1",
  "event": "validation_complete",
  "timestamp": "<ISO-8601>",
  "repository": "<owner/repo>",
  "issue_number": <number | null>,
  "stellar_address": "<first-4...last-4>",
  "result": {
    "valid": <boolean>,
    "account_funded": <boolean>,
    "trustline_exists": <boolean>,
    "xlm_balance": "<string>",
    "checks": [{ "label": "<string>", "passed": <boolean> }]
  }
}
```

---

## Test output

```
PASS __tests__/webhook.test.ts
  computeWebhookSignature
    ✓ returns sha256= prefix
    ✓ produces deterministic signatures for same input
    ✓ produces different signatures for different secrets
    ✓ produces different signatures for different payloads
    ✓ matches a known HMAC-SHA256 value
  buildWebhookPayload
    ✓ redacts the stellar address
    ✓ sets schema_version to "1"
    ✓ sets event to validation_complete
    ✓ includes issue_number
    ✓ accepts null issue_number
    ✓ maps result fields correctly for passing run
    ✓ maps result fields correctly for failing run
    ✓ maps checks array
    ✓ includes repository
    ✓ includes a valid ISO-8601 timestamp
  deliverWebhook
    ✓ returns sent=true with statusCode on success
    ✓ sends the X-TrustBridge-Signature header when secret is set
    ✓ does NOT send the signature header when no secret
    ✓ returns sent=false on network error without throwing
    ✓ returns sent=false on AbortError (timeout) without throwing
    ✓ sends to the correct URL
    ✓ sends Content-Type: application/json
    ✓ signature matches computed value for the same body
  sendWebhookNotification
    ✓ does nothing when webhookUrl is empty
    ✓ completes without throwing when webhook fails

Tests: 25 passed
```

body:
`run-gedcom-roundtrip.ps1`'s stability check used `SHA256.HashData` and `Convert.ToHexString`, both .NET 5+ only. Windows PowerShell 5.1 runs on .NET Framework and has neither, so running the script (or `run-tests-coverage.ps1`, which calls it) from a plain `powershell.exe` terminal failed with `MethodNotFound`.

Swapped for `SHA256.Create()` + `ComputeHash` and `BitConverter.ToString` (stripped of its `-` separators), both available on .NET Framework and modern .NET. Verified the kennedy sample gives an identical PASS/PASS result under both `powershell.exe` and `pwsh`.

author: cardinal-1986
body: ## The thing I got wrong in PR #23 PR #23 signs photos baked into documents. I tested it with fixtures shaped `{ path, url }` and it passed. **Those objects do not exist in this database.** ```sql select (el ? 'path') as has_path, (el ? 'storage_path') as has_storage_path from estimates e, jsonb_array_elements(e.photos::jsonb) el; -- 5 rows, all false / false ``` The picker builds estimate photos from `{ photo_id, url, caption }` only. So `estimatePhotoPaths()` returned `[]` for every real estimate, `signedPhotoMap([])` returned `{}`, and `docPhotoUrl` fell through to `p.url` - the raw public URL. Correct code fed an empty list. Proven by running the shipped functions against the real shape: ``` estimatePhotoPaths(real estimate) -> [] docPhotoUrl(...) -> https://.../object/public/photos/... is it signed? NO ``` Had the bucket flipped after #23, **every photo in every document would have broken.** ## The fix: derive the path instead of migrating ```sql select count(*), (split_part(data,'/object/public/photos/',2) = storage_path) from project_photos where storage_path <> '' group by 2; -- 215 | true <- no exceptions select count(*) from project_photos where storage_path ~ '[^A-Za-z0-9._~/-]'; -- 0 <- decodeURIComponent is a safe inverse ``` `photoPathOf()` now falls back to parsing the path out of the URL. This repairs **every historical row with no migration**, and needs no backfill I could get wrong. `/object/sign/` is accepted too, so an already-signed URL stays re-signable. Base64 `data:` URIs yield `null` and keep rendering inline. The picker also writes `path` onto new objects now - belt-and-braces, but it makes new rows self-describing rather than dependent on a URL shape. ## The builder strip The last in-app render on a raw public URL. `renderPhotos()` is synchronous, so the signed URLs land in a module-state map and get **painted onto the `` nodes** instead of triggering a re-render - a re-render would destroy a caption someone is halfway through typing. Keyed on `data-pi`, so reordering photos cannot mis-assign one. 1-hour TTL here (editing surface), not the 10-year document TTL. ## Verification - 5 anchors unique · scope proof reproduces the file byte-for-byte · bytes outside `cr-est-script` and the `photoPathOf` body identical - 20 assertions, incl. all **four** pre-existing `photoPathOf` call sites surviving verbatim (its contract widened underneath them) - `node --check` on **99/99** inline scripts · script/style tags balanced - **32 behaviour tests** against the real DB shape: derivation exact, one bulk request per gallery, reorder-safety, no redundant re-sign, and `estimates.photos` objects provably unmutated (`saveEstimate()` persists them verbatim, so writing an expiring URL onto one would corrupt the record) ## After this Every render and every document bake resolves a signature. The bucket can flip private - which is what actually invalidates any path list harvested while enumeration was open.

# Description
orb-service [PR #1963 ](https://github.com/circleci/orb-service/pull/1963) changes how serial job-groups and single-job serial-groups compile: a group-end no-op now gates downstream jobs on leaf/job success, while the unlock (serial-end) job dangles off it and always runs to release the lock. Previously downstream jobs were wired to unlock and ran regardless of outcome.

This clarifies to users the new behaviour.

author: myleshorton
body:
New **`flint-proxyless`** crate — the Rust counterpart to the Outline SDK smart dialer's proxyless path (`x/smart`, `findDNS × findTLS`): reach the **real destination** with no proxy and no exit hop, by finding a `(resolver, wire)` pairing the local network does not block. Chunk 2 of the proxyless port. [#13](https://github.com/getlantern/flint/pull/13) made the DNS and shaping axes orthogonal; this consumes them as a genuine cartesian product. ## The certificate is the oracle This is the load-bearing idea, so it is worth stating before the mechanics. A censor can block a connection, and can answer a plaintext DNS query with anything it likes. What it **cannot** do is produce a valid certificate for the destination. So the test for "did this strategy work" is not *did DNS answer* or *did TCP connect* — it is **did a TLS handshake to the resolved address complete against a verified chain and hostname**. Every dial in this crate, probe and destination alike, uses `CertVerification::Roots`. An unverified dial would destroy the property the whole design rests on. Note this is deliberately **stricter than the legacy resolver dial**, which still inherits `CertVerification::None` (design §11, the follow-up from #13). That oracle is also what admits the poisonable resolver kinds here even though `default_pool()` excludes them: a forged answer cannot survive the handshake, so a poisoned resolver *loses the race* rather than silently winning it. ```mermaid flowchart TB S["Space — resolvers × wires"] --> E["enumerate wire-major
all resolvers on no-op plan first"] E --> R["race_windowed, window = 4"] R --> P["probe candidate"] subgraph ORACLE["probe — the oracle"] direction TB P1["resolve domain via Kind + WirePlan
flint_dns::resolve_one_shaped"] P2["dial resolved IP with the same WirePlan"] P3["verify chain + hostname
CertVerification::Roots"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 end P --> ORACLE ORACLE -->|"all test domains pass"| W["winning Strategy"] ORACLE -.->|"any domain fails"| X["candidate abandoned"] W --> C["StrategyCache — resolver name + wire index
re-verified on next use, never trusted"] W --> D["dial host:port — verified destination stream"] ``` ## Search behaviour, and why **Wire-major enumeration.** Every resolver against the no-op plan first, then against each shaping plan in turn. That settles "is any resolver reachable with no shaping at all" before paying for shaping — the same instinct as the smart dialer resolving DNS before searching TLS transports. **A window of 4.** Each probe is a real DNS lookup plus a real TLS handshake. Firing dozens at once would be slow, wasteful, and conspicuous on exactly the networks that are watching. `race_windowed` refills as each finishes, so the common case (an early candidate works) never touches the tail. There is a test asserting peak in-flight never exceeds the window. **All test domains, not any.** One domain might be reachable by accident while the network is still hostile to the rest, so a partial pass must not win. An empty domain list is rejected outright rather than trivially "succeeding" against everything — a search with no oracle proves nothing. **A cached winner is re-verified, not trusted.** What worked yesterday may be blocked today. On a cache hit the strategy is re-probed; if that fails the entry is forgotten and the full search runs, so a strategy the censor has since caught cannot pin the client to a dead path. `StrategyCache` stores a `(resolver name, wire index)` pair — both plain values a caller can persist with whatever encoding it already uses, and the stable resolver name survives pool reordering or a signed pool update. A stale entry resolves to `None` rather than to the wrong strategy. ## Testability The verification step is injectable (`find_with` / `find_cached_with`), so the search *logic* — enumeration order, the all-domains rule, concurrency bounds, failure reporting, cache hit/miss/self-heal — is unit-tested with **no network and no TLS engine**. That matters here because `flint_dial::dial` needs the `boring` feature, which the default CI job does not enable; without injection none of this would be covered by `cargo test --workspace`. The real end-to-end path is a `#[ignore]`d live test (`live_find_reaches_real_domains`), matching the existing convention in `flint-dns`. ## Scope, stated plainly No exit hop means traffic leaves the user's own address for the real destination. This defeats **blocking**, not **observation** — an on-path censor still sees which host is being contacted, it just cannot classify or cut the TLS — and it does nothing against IP-level blackholing. It is a reachability tool, not an anonymity one, and must not silently stand in for a proxy path a user believes is carrying their traffic. This is in the crate docs and design §6.2 so it cannot be missed by a future caller. ## Verification - `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean - `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean - `cargo test --workspace` — clean; **12 flint-proxyless tests** (1 live-ignored) - `cargo doc -p flint-proxyless` — **zero warnings** - `cargo check -p flint-proxyless --features boring` — clean (the live path's engine wiring) ## Next Chunk 3 is `disorder`/TTL as a new shaping axis, and the spark-side transport plus `Kindling::with_proxyless` for config fetches follow. The §11 resolver-verification gap from #13 remains the highest-value separate follow-up — this crate does not depend on it being fixed, since it verifies its own dials, but the legacy DoH path still does not. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_01BufGsK81otiqihvrZdfoJX ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Added proxyless connectivity that searches DNS resolver and TLS connection strategies. * Verifies candidate connections across all configured test domains before selecting a strategy. * Added bounded parallel probing to find working strategies efficiently. * Added per-network caching with automatic validation and recovery from stale entries. * **Documentation** * Documented proxyless strategy selection, verification, caching, and limitations.

body: Split out of #2072, which didn't work out visually as a whole. This is the map-label half of #2066, on its own and without the colour-stripe work. ## What changed - Draw one non-interactive route label per ride on the directions map's transit lines, using the shared route-badge layout and both flavors' existing badge renderer. - Resolve each leg's stroke once and share it between the leg's polyline and its label, so a label can't end up a different colour from the line it names. - Give `RouteBadge` an `interactive` flag; both renderers register only an interactive label as a tap target. ## Why A drawn itinerary's transit lines said nothing about which route they were — the rider had to match a colour on the map to a badge in the drawer beside it. The focused-stop adjacency view already solved this with anchored route labels, so the same layout is reused here: labels sit at stable distance midpoints and stagger apart when two ridden corridors overlap. The labels are informational rather than tappable. Adjacency labels navigate to their route, but a directions label names a leg of the trip the rider is already reading, so a stray tap must not drop the whole itinerary for a single route's map. Legs of one route share a single label, keyed by wire route id — or, on an OTP1 response, which names a route without identifying it, by the name the leg displays. A route that names itself in no way at all, and a line too short to anchor on, are simply left unlabelled. This PR deliberately does **not** change any leg's colour: a ride still keeps its agency's hue via `itineraryLegStyle`. author: alisonjenkins
body:
An HTTPS-only deployment was advertising itself over plain HTTP:

```json
{"LocalAddress": "http://prototype.aliflix.alison-jenkins.com", ...}
```

Right host, wrong scheme. `LocalAddress` is what clients are told to use when publishing a reachable URL to peers (casting, SyncPlay, native clients) — so anything that followed it dropped to plaintext, or was blocked as mixed content on an HTTPS page.

## Not pharos's fault
pharos reads the scheme through actix's `ConnectionInfo`, which honours `X-Forwarded-Proto` correctly. The angie config in front set that header to `$scheme` — and since TLS terminates at the cluster gateway and angie's own listener is plaintext, `$scheme` is `http`. The proxy overwrote the gateway's truthful `https` with its own.

Isolated by sending the header to each hop in turn:

| hop | `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` sent | LocalAddress |
|---|---|---|
| straight to pharos | yes | `https://` ✅ |
| through angie | yes | `http://` ❌ |

## Fix
Honour an inbound value via a `map`, falling back to `$scheme` only when the header is absent — so a deployment with nothing in front still describes itself correctly. In the shared `mkAngieUi`, so the pharos-ui pod gets it too.

Verified against the live server through both configs before shipping:

| config | header | result |
|---|---|---|
| new | `https` | `https://` ✅ |
| new | absent | `http://` ✅ correct fallback |
| old | `https` | `http://` ❌ |

The same clobber fed every other `connection_info().scheme()` caller, including `dlna::base_url_from_request`.

## Test
`the_advertised_address_follows_the_clients_scheme` pins the **server** half of the contract in-tree. The proxy half lives in `flake.nix` and has no test harness — so the half that can regress silently is the half a repo test can hold.

`just test`: 1855 passed. `nix flake check` passes. clippy `-D warnings` clean.

## Deployment note
Like B162, this ships in `pharos-jellyfin-web`, which is pinned to a commit SHA with `pullPolicy: IfNotPresent` — it needs the GitOps pin bumped to deploy.

author: brain-crystal
body:
Lets Verify drive a running instance of a branch in a real browser instead of only reading the diff.

Ported from the setup running on `aviator-ag-org/excalidraw`. Everything the preview depends on is identical between the two repos — yarn, `publicDir: "../public"`, the `VITE_APP_PORT || 3000` logic, and **vite pinned at 5.0.12** — so the only content change was the baked clone URL.

## What's here

| File | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `docker/preview/Dockerfile` | The pre-warmed machine. Paste into Aviator to build the e2b template — it is never read from the repo. |
| `.aviator/scripts/preview-setup.sh` | Builds and starts the app at launch |
| `.aviator/verify/skills/default.md` | Guidance for the verify agent |

## How the caching works

The image bakes `node_modules` (~871 MB). At launch Aviator cleans the tree with `git reset --hard` + `git clean -fd` — **no `-x`** — so gitignored paths survive. That is the entire caching mechanism. The setup script reinstalls only when the branch touched `package.json`/`yarn.lock`, diffing against the commit recorded in `/preview-image-sha` (kept outside `/code` so the clean cannot delete it).

## Things that are load-bearing

- **The clone URL must match the connected repo.** Aviator compares `/code`'s origin against the repo name; on a mismatch it does not error — it deletes `/code` and re-clones, destroying the cache with nothing in the logs to explain it.
- **`--host 0.0.0.0`** — the browser driving the preview runs on Aviator's side, not in the sandbox. Loopback-only looks healthy in the logs while being unreachable.
- **`--port 3000` explicitly** — `.env.development` sets `VITE_APP_PORT=3001`, so the apparent default is not the real one.
- **`--strictPort`** — otherwise vite silently shifts to the next free port, which Aviator does not expose.
- **vite is pinned at 5.0.12.** Any bump past 5.4.12 activates the dev-server Host check and blocks `*.e2b.app` until `server.allowedHosts` is set.

## No seed data

The canvas starts empty, which is excalidraw's genuine first-run state. Scenes live in browser `localStorage` rather than on a server, so there is nothing the setup script could seed from inside the sandbox — and the alternative (having the page seed itself via an injected script) is more machinery than this repo needs. A scenario that needs shapes draws them.

The verify skill says so explicitly, so the agent does not treat an empty canvas as a failed load.

## Not wired up by this PR

Merging is necessary but not sufficient — runbooks branch off `master`, so these files have to be here first. Still needed on the Aviator side: connect the repo, build the template from the Dockerfile, and add the `verify.preview` config pointing at it on port 3000.

author: srobroek
body:
## Summary

- Releasing a lease previously needed a timer or a guess. `SubagentStop` carries the same `agent_type` values as `SubagentStart`, so a hook can match the claim-holder roles and know a node actor just exited. The exit itself is the evidence, with no liveness inference.
- A stop is not an ending, though. `domain-specialist` is explicitly resumable and its review/fix loop depends on being woken for the same node, so clearing the binding on every stop would strand a live actor between review rounds. `SubagentStop` cannot distinguish finished from paused; only the activation resource can.
- So `subagent-exit` is a trigger rather than an actor. It stamps `exited` on the checkout and releases the binding only when `stale_binding` already proves the work is over: resource closed, or unassigned and no longer in progress. The stamp is what lets a later prune be event-driven instead of a periodic sweep.

## Verification

Fired against live state for a specialist whose node sits `in_progress` and unassigned as a review handoff. `exited` was recorded and the binding survived, which is the case that would otherwise brick a resumable actor.

Six tests cover the resumable case, the resolved case, an unknown context, a missing context, and two failure paths. The hook always exits 0, because a stop hook that fails would trap the subagent it fires for. 284 tests pass.

## Follow-up, not included

Pruning a worktree once its work has landed keys on the shepherd's `merge_sha`, already durable on the merge bead, so it needs a pass that reads it rather than a new notification mechanism.

Worth flagging separately: `wt step prune` is not lease-aware. At `--min-age 0s` it offers live leased checkouts for deletion, and only the 1-day default currently prevents that.

author: jiwenc-nv
body:
## What

`isaacteleop`'s authored Python moves from seven scattered `src/` trees into one `src/python/isaacteleop/`; the ten `*_init.py` shims become real `__init__.py`. All C++ stays put, pybind TUs included.

## Why

`pip install -e .` was not editable: with no `wheel.packages` mapping, scikit-build-core emitted `known_source_files = {}`, so every module resolved to a site-packages copy (#735). Adding a subpackage needed three registrations, and `cloudxr_exp` duplicated `cloudxr` at build time.

## Commit order is load-bearing

`35f938ec` must precede `55f07568`: the shims ship unconditionally, so under the old module-presence probe `_is_exp_available()` returns true on every Orin install (T234 defaults on) and `get_sdk_path()` then raises — breaking `python -m isaacteleop.cloudxr` for released-wheel users.

## Compatibility

Released-wheel delta vs `main`, sha256-verified across every member: **two added** (`cloudxr_exp/{__init__,runtime}.py` — that bundle defaults off, so they were never shipped) and **two changed** (`cloudxr/runtime.py`, the probe rewrite; and a corrected docstring in `retargeters/sharpa_hand_retargeter.py`). Nothing removed. Import paths, `.so`/`.pyi` placement and `python -m` entry points untouched. The `BUILD_VIZ` guard drops `viz/__init__.py` from the staged tree, where it shipped without its `.so`; the released wheel already omitted it.

## Verification

`ctest` 160/160 after every commit. Editable install: `known_source_files` `{}` → 95 entries, `known_wheel_files` holds zero `.py`, and the sets are disjoint — the invariant that matters, since `find_spec` prefers wheel files.

Please confirm in CI what I could not build locally: `BUNDLE_ROBOTIC_GROUNDING=ON` and `ENABLE_CLOUDXR_EXP_BUNDLE=ON`.

Closes #735.

author: carolsimone
body:
## The problem

On a fresh bundled install, `manifest-controller` crash-loops. Observed repeatedly, including in the Task 12 cold-start test:

```
manifest-controller-b46f9968b-bs786  0/1  Error              4 (58s ago)  4m2s
manifest-controller-b46f9968b-bs786  0/1  CrashLoopBackOff   4 (8s ago)   4m10s
manifest-controller-b46f9968b-bs786  1/1  Running            5 (92s ago)  5m34s
```

It is the only service that does this — and it is the only one whose dependencies the existing gate does not cover.

## Root cause

`deployment.yaml` emitted `initContainers:` only under:

```
{{- if and $.Values.postgresql.enabled $svc.env $svc.env.POSTGRES_DB }}
```

`manifest-controller`'s values declare `REDIS_URL`, `REDIS_PASSWORD`, and S3 credentials — **no `POSTGRES_DB`**. So the condition was false, it got no gate at all, started before the bundled Redis StatefulSet was reachable, and died on connect.

`ui-service` has the same shape and the same exposure.

## Why it costs more than it looks

CrashLoopBackOff backoff is exponential — 10s, 20s, 40s, 80s, 160s. By the fifth restart the pod idles over two minutes, well after Redis is ready. **The restart loop costs more time than the wait it replaces**, and it makes the README's `kubectl get pods -w` show `Error` and `CrashLoopBackOff` to someone evaluating the project for the first time.

## The fix

Two conditions instead of one, with a `wait-for-redis` initContainer (a `redis-cli ping` loop, 3s interval, 100-try ceiling) mirroring the existing `wait-for-migrations`.

Rendering verified in both modes:

| Mode | manifest-controller | ui-service | Postgres-backed services |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| bundled | `[wait-for-redis]` | `[wait-for-redis]` | `[wait-for-migrations]` |
| BYO | `[]` | `[]` | `[]` |

BYO renders nothing, correctly — those installs point at Redis that is already running, so a gate would be pure delay.

## A gap left deliberately

The condition keys on `REDIS_URL`, which covers exactly the services lacking a Postgres gate. Services holding `REDIS_PASSWORD` without `REDIS_URL` (the Go services build the URL differently) all carry `wait-for-migrations`, and Postgres plus Flyway takes longer than Redis becoming ready — so they are already gated in practice. Adding a second initContainer and image pull to seven services to close a race that cannot currently happen would cost more than it returns.

## How it was verified

`bash scripts/install-test/lint.sh` → **OK across all 4 topologies**.

A local kind install confirmed the behaviour change: **total restarts across all pods = 0**, with `manifest-controller` sitting at `Init:0/1`.

**Honest limitation:** that local run did not complete — `helm install rc=1` after 901s, because the host (colima, 6 CPU / 7.7 GiB, already running another kind cluster and a 4-container trino stack) could not schedule the datastores, which stayed `Pending`.

That is arguably a *sharper* test than a happy path: the datastores never became available at all, which is precisely the condition that previously produced five crashes. Old behaviour — crash repeatedly. New behaviour — wait quietly. But it is not a green end-to-end install, and I am not claiming one. **CI's `install-test.yml` is the authoritative gate here** and runs on chart-path changes.

## Versioning

PATCH — template fix, no values contract change. Changelog entry added under `## [Unreleased]`.

## Checklist

- [x] Commit is signed off
- [x] `scripts/install-test/lint.sh` passes across 4 topologies
- [x] `deploy/continuo/CHANGELOG.md` updated under `[Unreleased]`
- [x] No `values.schema.json` change needed — no values keys added, renamed, or removed
- [x] No `docs/arch/*` impact: no service behavior, interface, storage, Redis flow, gRPC, or S3 change — this is startup ordering only

author: wilfordgrimley
body:
## The finding

All five tests in `TestImplicitVoteCapForm` pass with the cap deleted — including the one named `test_implicit_weight_is_hard_capped_per_outcome_group`.

**Mutation, verified:** delete the `min(...)` from `vote_consensus.py:505` so `full_weight` returns the raw implicit sum. All 92 tests in `test_vote_consensus.py` stay green. `PRINTING_TAG_IMPLICIT_CAP` appears in exactly two files repo-wide, so nothing else could catch it. The cap was untested dead code under every test that named it.

## Why it matters

An implicit vote is a **passive acceptance**, and the trigger is the filter chip:

> a low-weight, hard-capped `IMPLICIT` vote cast passively when someone picks a candidate under an active `/editor` filter chip
> — `docs/identification-pipeline.md:234`

The person picked a card. They never tapped "yes, this tag applies". The invariant is that **passive acceptance never decides** — twenty people quietly taking the suggestion the UI put in front of them is not the same evidence as one person deliberately voting, and must never add up to more.

Ratified as D5/S3 in the owner-ratified 2026-07-22 vote-weight scenario matrix (`docs/reference/vote-weight-matrix.md`, implemented in PR #325). Narrative form in `docs/theory.md:254-260` (§4 soundness mechanisms) and `docs/features/printing-tags.md`'s implicit-vote section.

## Why the old tests could not see it

**Two independent mechanisms** enforce the invariant, and every cell was landing on the wrong one:

| | mechanism | what it stops |
|---|---|---|
| (a) | `VoteSource.IMPLICIT` ∈ `_MACHINE_DERIVED_SOURCES` | implicit weight can never satisfy the `has_human_backed` gate, however much piles up |
| (b) | **the cap** | implicit weight can never supply the **quorum** weight alone |

`vote_consensus.py`'s own comment on that set says (a) *"is what stops it from ever supplying the human-backed bit, **which the cap alone would not**"*. They are deliberately belt-and-braces — and that is exactly what made the cap invisible to testing:

- **C1** (no human vote at all) is decided by (a) at the `winner["has_human_backed"]` check, before the cap is consulted.
- **C2, C4, and the old "hard capped" cell** put 2 human votes (weight 1.0) on the winning side. That sets `exclude_non_human = True` via D4's human-quorum exclusion, which discards *all* non-human weight **before** `full_weight` — the cap's only call site — is ever reached.

Both shapes pass identically with the cap deleted.

## What this adds

Two cells in the shape where the cap is the deciding mechanism: exactly one human-backed group whose human weight alone stays *below* `min_weight`, so a real person has satisfied the gate and the only question left is whether passive acceptance can finish the job. Written as scenarios, not arithmetic.

**`test_passive_acceptances_cannot_finish_the_quorum_one_real_voter_started`**
One deliberate vote for A, then sixteen people picking that candidate under a chip endorsing A, against `min_weight=3`.

```
capped:   1.0 + min(4.0, 1.0) = 2.0  -> short of quorum, stays unresolved
uncapped: 1.0 +      4.0      = 5.0  -> resolves on accumulated passive picks
```

`min_weight=3` rather than the usual 2 on purpose: at 2, one human vote plus a fully-capped pile lands *exactly* on quorum (1.0 + 1.0), which is decision D2's deliberate promotion path — a real ruling, but it makes that cell unable to tell capped from uncapped.

**`test_passive_acceptances_cannot_outrank_the_one_person_who_actually_voted`**
One deliberate vote for A plus four passive picks endorsing A, against forty passive picks endorsing B that no human ever asserted.

```
capped:   A = 1.0 + min(1.0, 1.0) = 2.0  vs  B = min(10.0, 1.0) = 1.0
          -> A selected, clears quorum, share 2/3, human-backed -> "A"
uncapped: A = 2.0                        vs  B = 10.0
          -> B selected; B has no human-backed weight -> returns None
```

Uncapped, the pile of passive picks does not win the card — it **de-resolves** it. A card a real person answered correctly is dragged back to unresolved by forty people who never answered anything. This is why the cap is per *outcome group* rather than a global bound.

**Both go red when the `min(...)` is deleted; the other 92 stay green.**

## Also, without changing behaviour

- Renamed the misleading cell to `test_implicit_dissent_volume_loses_to_d4_exclusion_not_to_the_cap`, and said in-line that the cap is unreached there. It is a real D4 test — just not the cap test its name claimed.
- Renamed C1 to `test_c1_repeated_picks_under_a_filter_chip_never_resolve_without_a_human_vote` (scenario framing, matrix cell reference preserved) and recorded that it passes via mechanism (a), so it is not mistaken for cap coverage.
- Class docstring now states the trigger, the invariant, both mechanisms, and the precondition a cap cell must meet — so the next cell added does not land in the same dead shape.

## Verification

- `cardpicker/tests/test_vote_consensus.py` — 94 passed (was 92).
- Full `cardpicker/tests/` suite green.
- No production code changed.

author: ovvo-financial
body:
## Summary

Adds `RHLean/Proof/SquareBlockCoherentGram.lean`.

This formalizes the exact cross-block Gram bridge discussed after PR #154. For the real square-block increments `Delta_j`, define the rank-one Gram kernel

```text
G(i,j) = Delta_i * Delta_j.
```

The coherent all-ones quadratic form through block `N` is

```text
sum_{i,j <= N} G(i,j).
```

The main theorem proves exactly

```text
coherentGramMass(N) = (sum_{j <= N} Delta_j)^2.
```

Thus any future estimate suppressing the coherent block mode immediately gives a quantitative cross-block cancellation bound.

## Theorems

- `squareBlockCoherentGramMass_eq_prefix_sq`
- `squareBlockCoherentGramMass_nonneg`
- `abs_realCanonicalTotalPrefix_le_sqrt_of_coherentGram_le`
- `normalized_prefix_sq_eq_normalized_coherentGram`

## Mathematical role

This is the precise bridge needed to combine:

- worst-case same-sign behavior inside each block;
- oscillation and negative correlation across blocks;
- a concrete Gram estimate on the all-ones mode.

It does not assume or claim the remaining arithmetic Gram suppression theorem. It makes that target exact:

```text
squareBlockCoherentGramMass N = o(N^2)
```

is equivalent to normalized cumulative square-block cancellation.

## Validation

GitHub Actions on the pinned Lean/mathlib toolchain is authoritative.

author: atbe
body:
## Why

E2E is the only suite that talks to a real provider, so it is the only one
that can catch a **wire-contract break** — a payload the engine builds
happily and the API rejects.

It was `workflow_dispatch` + `workflow_call` only, and the sole caller was
`engine--release.yml`. So a change could pass every PR check and still be
structurally incapable of working, failing for the first time at the
release gate.

That is not hypothetical: it is exactly how `cache_control` on a Responses
content block got merged and then failed the v0.3.0 release run with
`400 unknown_parameter`. Unit and integration tests asserted the shape the
engine *produces*, never the shape the API *accepts*, and the local stack
routes through LiteLLM, which tolerates the extra key. Nothing on the PR
path made a direct-to-OpenAI call.

## Change

Adds a `pull_request` trigger with the same `paths` filter the
integration-tests workflow uses, so it only fires when engine code or its
build inputs change.

## Tradeoff

This costs one live-provider run per relevant PR. The alternative is
discovering wire breaks at release time, which is later, more disruptive,
and blocks the release rather than the PR. Worth it.

This PR exercises the new trigger on itself — the workflow file is in its
own `paths` filter.

author: ondrejvatka
body:
Clears the fixable Dependabot advisories and records why the remaining three stay.

Closes FO-15.

## Fixed

| Package | Severity | How |
|---|---|---|
| fast-uri | 2 × high | lockfile refresh (transitive under the MCP SDK) |
| hono | 3 × moderate | lockfile refresh |
| @hono/node-server | moderate | lockfile refresh |
| body-parser | low | lockfile refresh |
| js-yaml, postcss | high | lockfile refresh (dev toolchain) |
| brace-expansion | high | override to `^5.0.8` (hoisted instances) |
| react-router | 2 × moderate | `react-router-dom` 6.30.4 → 7.18.2 |

The two React Router advisories are the ones that actually mattered — open redirect (GHSA-wrjc-x8rr-h8h6) and open redirect leading to XSS (GHSA-jjmj-jmhj-qwj2), both reachable from a browser SPA. **GHSA-jjmj has no fix on the 6.x line at all**, so remaining on 6 meant permanent exposure.

The major needed two migration fixes: the `future` opt-ins no longer exist as props (both are default behaviour in 7), and `navigate` returns a promise, so the click handler now discards it explicitly.

## Left in place, deliberately

**react-router GHSA-qwww-vcr4-c8h2 (high)** — affects `>=7.12.0 <8.3.0`, and 8.3.0 is unreleased, so no fixed version exists. It's an RSC-mode CSRF bypass; this is a Vite SPA on `BrowserRouter` with no RSC, so the path never executes. npm proposes downgrading to 7.11.0 — that would reintroduce both open-redirect advisories above, trading two applicable browser vulnerabilities for one that cannot fire here.

**brace-expansion GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg (high)**, one instance — the advisory is `<= 5.0.7` with first patched 5.0.8, so every 1.x and 2.x release is in range and only the 5.x line was patched. The override reaches everything except `workbox-build → ejs → jake → filelist → minimatch@5.1.9`, which npm won't rewrite. Build-time only, and the DoS needs attacker-supplied glob patterns where the only globs are this repo's own config.

**esbuild GHSA-g7r4-m6w7-qqqr (low)** — unchanged from f087c75. tsup@8.5.1 is still latest and still pins `^0.27.0`, where everything from 0.27.3 up is affected. Needs esbuild's dev server on Windows; tsup only calls the build API.

## Verification

typecheck, lint, 48 tests, format:check, both workspace builds (tsup and vite), the icon generator against sharp 0.35.3 (output re-verified as valid PNGs at correct dimensions, then reverted to keep binary churn out of this PR), and the UI in a real browser — login renders and a deep link to `/ticket/:ref` still redirects through `ProtectedRoute` with a clean console.

## Summary

- add field-only `@gql.authorizationUnchecked({reason})` migration coverage
- expose unchecked fields in the authorization manifest with reason and source location

## Safety

1. ALUA failover churn (the qla2xxx ISP error recovery, target re-enables, NEXUS_LOSS) causes the backing devices to stack up reset Unit Attentions. You can see them arriving: `sd 18:0:0:3: Power-on or device reset occurred` at 259.4s and again at 269.961s.  The BUG fires at 269.968s, 7 ms later, on thread `18:0:0:31_0`, which is the SCST device thread for pass-through device `18:0:0:31` (dev_disk in HA forwarding mode, H:C:T:L-named devices, same scheme as the Created DLM lockspace ... for 17:0:0:4 line).
2. The initiator (Cisco UCS WWPNs which are almost certainly ESXi issuing VMFS ATS heartbeats) sends COMPARE AND WRITE so SCST emulates it with an internal READ(16) first, compare, then WRITE(16).
3. At parse time, a READ command gets `resp_data_len = bufflen` (scst_targ.c:1355-1359).512 bytes for a 1-block CAW, which matches `RDX=0x200` in the oops (and `RAX=2 = CHECK_CONDITION`).
4. The internal READ is executed via pass-through and comes back CHECK CONDITION with the unit-attention sense. The pass-through completion path, `scst_do_cmd_done()` at scst_targ.c:2175, copies the SCSI status directly into `cmd->status` and never touches `resp_data_len`. Compare with the path virtual devices use `scst_set_cmd_error_status()` at scst_lib.c:1778 explicitly zeroes `resp_data_len` which is why vdisk-backed LUNs can never trip this and the bug survived so long. The stale `scst_dev_check_set_UA` frame in the backtrace corroborates this. That's `scst_pass_through_cmd_done()` (scst_targ.c:3157) propagating the UA sense it just received, moments before the fatal call.
5. `scst_finish_internal_cmd()` invokes `scst_cwr_read_cmd_finished()`, sees `status != 0` with `resp_data_len == 512`, and the `sBUG` panics the box.

## Summary
Closes #34. Cross-checked every list/detail serializer's returned fields against what the frontend actually consumes (grepped each `.field` read in the relevant page/component), then dropped anything with zero consumers:

- **Reminders**: `ReminderListSerializer` down from 20 fields to the 11 `ReminderCard.jsx` uses. `ReminderDetailSerializer` no longer inherits from `ReminderListSerializer` — the edit form (`ReminderDetailsForm.jsx`) needs a different field set (`catalog_key`, `tracking_method`, intervals, `notes`) than the list view (`status`/`message`/`progress_percent`), so they're now independent, purpose-built serializers instead of a superset relationship. Also dropped `next_due_odometer_km`/`next_due_date` from the `services/reminders.py` digest dicts (`build_service_reminder`/`build_inspection_reminder`) — unread by any consumer of `GET /services/reminders/`.
- **Expenses / Inspections / Services**: trimmed each list serializer to its actual consumer's fields (`frontend/app/expenses/page.jsx`, `frontend/app/cars/[id]/page.jsx`).
- **Cars**: `CarListSerializer`/`CarDetailSerializer` trimmed — `display_name` and `is_active` had zero references anywhere in the frontend.
- **Assistant**: `ConversationListSerializer` down to just `id` (only used to chain into a detail fetch); `ConversationDetailSerializer` down to `id, messages`. Also dropped a now-pointless `select_related("car")` query hint since neither serializer reads `car` anymore.
- **Accounts**: `UserProfileSerializer` (used standalone and embedded as `"user"` in every auth response) dropped `full_name`, `role`, `is_email_verified`, `date_joined` — none read anywhere. Kept `id` — `frontend/lib/telemetry.js` reads `getUser()?.id`, which the original issue audit missed.

Left `ExpenseDetailSerializer`, `InspectionDetailSerializer`, `ServiceRecordDetailSerializer`, and `UserListSerializer` untouched: confirmed none has any frontend consumer at all (no detail GET/PATCH call exists for the first three; the last is admin-only), so there was no basis to trim them further without more context on other consumers.

author: pepone
body:
## Summary

`ice_locatorCacheTimeout` and `ice_invocationTimeout` now normalize their argument in JavaScript, the same way
#6235 made them normalize in C++, C# and Java:

- Any negative timeout means infinite and is normalized to -1.
- A positive timeout that is not a whole number of the corresponding proxy property's unit (seconds for
  `LocatorCacheTimeout`, milliseconds for `InvocationTimeout`) is rounded up to the next whole number.
- A timeout greater than 2147483647 of that unit is rejected with a `RangeError`, as is a value that is not a
  number.

JavaScript was left out of #6235 because it has no duration-typed overload — but its single `number` parameter is
a float, so it played exactly the role `TimeSpan` plays in C#, and it had the same defect: a fractional timeout was
stored verbatim and `proxyToProperty` emitted `LocatorCacheTimeout=1.5`, which `propertyToProxy` then rejected with
`PropertyException`.

| call | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ice_invocationTimeout(0)` | `RangeError` | 0 (no timeout) |
| `ice_invocationTimeout(-2)` | `RangeError` | -1 |
| `ice_invocationTimeout(1.5)` | stored as 1.5 | 2 |
| `ice_invocationTimeout(2147483648)` | every invocation fails after ~1 ms | `RangeError` |
| `ice_invocationTimeout(Infinity)` | every invocation fails after ~1 ms | `RangeError` |
| `ice_invocationTimeout(NaN)` | stored as `NaN` | `RangeError` |
| `ice_invocationTimeout("10")` | stored as the string `"10"` | `RangeError` |
| `ice_locatorCacheTimeout(3e9)` | accepted, not representable as a property | `RangeError` |

The lower-bound rejections are gone. JavaScript's `newTimeout < 1 && newTimeout !== -1` predicate is the original
ICE-3492 check from 2014, which every mapping shared until #2794 / #2809 / #2810 removed it from C++, C# and Java
in September 2024 and left JavaScript behind. This restores the single contract.

## The property path

Unlike the other three mappings, no `toProperty` backstop is needed here: `ReferenceFactory.js` clamps
property-sourced values to -1 with a warning — the code #2810 removed from Java — so the per-proxy property path
cannot inject an unnormalized value. That is also why the `#6112` TODO comments added in #6235 have no JavaScript
counterpart.

That clamp did need one adjustment. It rejected `0` for `InvocationTimeout` and defaulted it to -1, which was
harmless while `0` was unreachable through the setter, but this PR makes `0` settable — so a proxy holding a zero
invocation timeout came back as infinite through `proxyToProperty` → `propertyToProxy`. The predicate is now
`< -1`, matching the locator cache timeout branch directly above it, and matching C++, which stores property
values unclamped. Per the discussion below, a follow-up will normalize `0` → -1 for the invocation timeout across
all mappings, which will revisit this.

## Tests

The existing negative-timeout assertions were vacuous and are replaced. `test()` throws `Error`, while each catch
clause tested the caught exception against a `TestError` class declared locally in `allTests` and never thrown, so
`test(!(ex instanceof TestError), ex)` was always `test(true)` — the block passed whatever the setters did. This is
the same shape @externl found in the Python, Ruby and MATLAB proxy tests during the #6235 review; those remain to
be fixed separately.

New assertions cover the normalized values, the rejected inputs, and — the case that was missing, and that let the
zero-timeout defect above ship in the first revision — a `proxyToProperty` → `propertyToProxy` round trip over
`[0, 0]`, `[2, 3]` and `[-1, -1]`.

Verified red → green twice: with the setter fix reverted, `Ice/proxy` fails at `ice_invocationTimeout(0)` with the

author: nasyrov
body:
In development a hydrating island now mounts with React `hydrateRoot` instead of `createRoot`, so a non-deterministic render (a `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, or locale read that differs between the Worker SSR pass and the browser) stops failing silently. React reconciles the client render against the server DOM, recovers by client-rendering the subtree — no crash — and fires one `onRecoverableError`. The renderer turns that into a `plumix:island-hydration-mismatch` window event carrying the island element and React's component stack, and the existing dev island-error overlay (#1603) renders it through the shared dev-error page, named and labeled by the island's component. A developer who ships a non-deterministic island now sees it flagged, by name, in the overlay they already know.

**Production is unchanged, byte-for-byte.** The `hydrateRoot` swap and the diagnostic live entirely inside the dev-only branch that `process.env.PLUMIX_DEV` (Vite-substituted to `""` in a build) strips out, so every island keeps mounting with `createRoot` in production.

This is the "prove the pipe end to end" slice of PRD #1666 — it deliberately stops short of the server-vs-client HTML **diff**, which is the PRD's next slice. So the overlay currently shows the component stack (which names the island) plus a synthesized message, not yet *what* diverged.

### Where to start reviewing

`packages/blocks/src/island-renderer.ts` is the one behavior seam. `mount()` now creates its React root **lazily on the first `render()`**: the first render hydrates (in dev), and a later `props`-attribute change reconciles as a plain re-render — never a re-hydration. That one-time distinction is the crux, and it's what keeps the custom element's re-render path (`island-element.ts`) unchanged.

### Notes for reviewers

- **`client="only"` islands** ship no server output, so they pass `hydrate: false` and mount with `createRoot` even in dev — never a mismatch source.
- **Crash vs. mismatch don't conflate.** Confirmed against React 19.2.7 + jsdom: a component throw during hydration fires `onUncaughtError` only (→ the existing `plumix:island-error` path), while a genuine DOM/text divergence fires `onRecoverableError` only. A render crash can't be mislabeled as a hydration mismatch.
- **Dev/prod runtime now differ by design.** `hydrateRoot` adopts the SSR DOM (preserving pre-hydration input/focus state) where `createRoot` blows it away and rebuilds. React recovers to the same final DOM on a mismatch, so nothing breaks; this is the spec's intent.
- The shared dev-error page drops its `(no stack available)` fallback when a component stack is the only signal, so a mismatch shows just the component-stack section rather than an empty, confusing "stack" block.

Tests extend the existing suites — the renderer mount contract (hydrate-vs-createRoot gate, mismatch dispatch, re-render-not-re-hydrate, client-only), the overlay (mismatch → shared page), and the dev-error page (fallback gating). No production behavior or markup changes.

Refs #1666
Fixes #1667
